changes.current_line: Billing that helps you grow revenue.
changes.change: For product-led buyers replacing a homegrown billing system: "Billing shouldn't be a tax on your roadmap. Ship pricing changes in minutes, not quarters."
changes.why: The champion pushed back on the revenue-growth line directly, saying they were trying to stop billing being 'a tax on the roadmap'. He reacted strongly to the demo as 'a quarter of roadmap in five minutes', which matches their real pain that every pricing change takes a quarter.

changes.current_line: Proven ROI, backed by an independent economic impact study.
changes.change: For deals where the CFO decides: in place of the generic study, offer "Your payback, in your numbers". This is a customer-specific cost-of-homegrown worksheet built from their engineering time on billing, billing errors and lapsed subscriptions. Send it within days of the first payback question, written for the CFO.
changes.why: The champion said he couldn't get the deal past the CFO 'without a number that's ours'. The generic ROI deck didn't answer his payback question, and the rep admitted they had the inputs but 'never added it up'.

changes.change: Add to the billing story for prospects migrating off a homegrown system: "Move your existing subscriptions without asking customers for their card details again, in stages, and around your renewal season." Back it with a named reference customer the prospect can call.
changes.why: The buyer's concrete migration needs were no re-collecting cards and a staged move, and he wanted to talk to someone who'd done it rather than read a doc.

changes.change: For status-quo deals where finance holds the budget, give champions a cost-of-inaction line to forward to finance: "Every pricing change costs us a quarter of roadmap, and the system's author has left. Here's what standing still costs per year: [their figure]." The aim is for the project to read as 'on fire' rather than 'nice to have'.
changes.why: The rival was doing nothing. Finance funded only what was 'on fire' and rated this a 'nice to have', and the real costs (a fragile system whose builder left, a quarter lost on every pricing change) were never put in front of finance.
